name: Cockatrice
description: The cockatrice is a legendary medieval European hybrid creature with the head, comb, and wattles of a rooster and the body and tail of a serpent or wyvern, said to kill with its breath, touch, or gaze and hatched from the yolkless egg of a cockerel incubated by a toad or snake.
full_description: The cockatrice is a legendary creature of medieval European bestiary tradition, conventionally depicted as a two-legged dragon or wyvern-like beast with the head, comb, wattles, and feet of a rooster (cock) and the long, scaled, serpentine tail of a snake or dragon. Its supposed powers include a deadly stare that kills or petrifies, poisonous breath, and a lethal touch — abilities largely shared with, and often identical to, those of the basilisk, with which the cockatrice is frequently conflated in late-medieval English usage. The creature is said to hatch from a yolkless ('cock's') egg laid by a seven-year-old rooster and incubated by a toad or serpent on a dunghill. Its weaknesses, according to medieval lore, include the crow of a rooster (which kills it instantly), the gaze of a weasel (the only animal immune to its own gaze), and its own reflection in a mirror. The English word 'cockatrice' was popularised by John Wycliffe's 1382 Bible translation, which used it to render Hebrew terms for venomous serpents in the Book of Isaiah and elsewhere. From the late 14th century onward the cockatrice appears in heraldry, in works of literature including Edmund Spenser's Faerie Queene and Shakespeare's Richard III and Romeo and Juliet, and in modern fantasy fiction. While zoologically a fiction, the figure is a long-attested feature of European cultural and religious history and remains a recognisable emblem of medieval monstrology.

aliases.name: Calcatrix
aliases.meaning: 'Tracker'; originally the Latin translation of Greek ichneumon

aliases.name: Basiliscus
aliases.meaning: Term for the basilisk often translated as 'cockatrice' in medieval English

aliases.name: Basilisk
aliases.meaning: Closely related and often interchangeable creature in medieval bestiaries

origin: A creature of medieval Western and Central European literary and bestiary tradition, with its widest attestation in England, France, the Low Countries, and the Holy Roman Empire. Through colonial-era and modern fantasy literature, the figure has spread to the entire Anglophone world.

etymology.origin: From Old French cocatris, ultimately from Medieval Latin calcatrix ('tracker'), itself a translation of Greek ichneumon ('tracker'), the Egyptian mongoose. The English word entered through Anglo-Norman in the 14th century.
etymology.meaning: Originally 'tracker' (referring to the mongoose's role in folklore as a hunter of crocodiles); by transfer in medieval Latin and Old French, the term came to denote the legendary basilisk-like beast.
etymology.first_use: Earliest English-language attestation is in John Wycliffe's Bible translation of 1382.

timeline.event: Alexander Neckam's De naturis rerum describes the basilisk as the offspring of a cock's egg incubated by a toad
timeline.significance: Foundational Latin description that English bestiaries inherit

timeline.event: Wycliffe's English Bible introduces 'cockatrice' as a translation for several Hebrew serpents in Isaiah 11, 14, 59 and Jeremiah 8
timeline.significance: Earliest English attestation of the word

timeline.event: John Trevisa translates Bartholomeus Anglicus, applying 'cockatrice' to the basilisk
timeline.significance: Cements the conflation of cockatrice with basilisk in English
timeline.source: Trevisa, J. (1397), translation of Bartholomeus Anglicus

timeline.event: A rooster is tried and burned at Basel for allegedly laying a cockatrice egg
timeline.significance: Famous early-modern instance of the legend acted upon socially and legally
timeline.source: E. P. Evans (1906), The Criminal Prosecution and Capital Punishment of Animals

timeline.event: Edmund Spenser, The Faerie Queene, references the cockatrice as a creature of evil enchantment
Shakespeare's Richard III refers to the 'cockatrice' eye as deadly
timeline.significance: Establishes the cockatrice as a Shakespearean rhetorical figure for malign gaze

timeline.event: Shakespeare's Romeo and Juliet refers to 'the death-darting eye of cockatrice'
timeline.significance: Anchors the cockatrice in popular Anglophone literary memory
timeline.source: Shakespeare, W., Romeo and Juliet III.ii

timeline.event: King James Bible retains 'cockatrice' from Wycliffe's tradition for several Old Testament passages
timeline.significance: Distributes the term to every English Protestant household

related.name: Basilisk
related.description: Closely related serpent monster; often used interchangeably with cockatrice in medieval and early modern English

related.name: Wyvern
related.description: Two-legged dragon of medieval heraldry; the cockatrice is structurally a wyvern with a rooster's head

related.name: Dragon
related.description: Broader medieval reptilian monster; the cockatrice belongs to the same tradition

related.name: Chimera
related.description: Greek hybrid monster of the same composite category

related.name: Gorgon
related.description: Petrifying-gaze ability shared with the cockatrice and basilisk

cultural_notes: The cockatrice was widely held in medieval Europe to be a real and exceedingly dangerous animal; superstitions involving its egg, its mirror-death, and its rooster-vulnerability persisted into the early modern period.
